title: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL
summary: This sub-technique covers abuse of dynamic link libraries (DLLs), the shared code files that Windows programs load at run time, and several distinct behaviours sit under the same label. Sideloading places a legitimate signed executable next to a malicious DLL carrying a name that executable expects, so the payload loads inside a trusted process. Search order hijacking plants a trojan DLL in a directory the loader checks before the real location. Phantom hijacking targets a module name that does not exist on disk, so any file with that name is accepted. Substitution overwrites a valid DLL in place, and redirection changes the search behaviour through registry settings or a redirection file. Many malicious libraries also forward their exports to the genuine library, which keeps the host application working and makes the change hard to notice. Detection rests on module load telemetry such as Sysmon event 7, file writes into program directories, and path or signature mismatches for loaded images.

beginner.definition: A dynamic link library is a shared file of code that many programs use. This sub-technique is about tricking a program into loading the wrong one. The attacker's file then runs as part of a trusted program. It is one branch of the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
beginner.whyItMatters: Programs are trusted because of who made them. A malicious library loaded by a trusted program may be allowed to run. The payload also gains that program's permissions. Some attackers hide the trick well, so the application still works. This makes the malware hard to spot with simple file checks.
howItWorks: A signed program is placed next to a malicious library file with a name it expects.
In search order hijacking, the malicious library sits in a folder the loader checks first.
Phantom hijacking targets a library name that is missing, so any file with that name loads.
Substitution replaces a real library with a malicious copy that has the same name.
Some malicious libraries also pass calls to the real library, so the program still runs.
Because the host program is trusted, the loaded code may avoid scrutiny.
beginner.example: Imagine a workshop where repairs always use a labelled box of spare parts. Nobody opens the box to check the parts, because the label is trusted. An attacker swaps the contents for a copy that looks identical and still fits. The machine keeps working, so the repair team notices nothing. A malicious library works the same way. It carries the expected name and sits where the program looks, so it is loaded without questions.
takeaways: A trusted program can load an untrusted library from the wrong folder.
Check where each loaded library came from, not only its file name.
A working application does not prove that its libraries are genuine.

objectives: Define a dynamic link library and explain why programs load them.
Describe sideloading, search order hijacking, phantom hijacking and substitution.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
Identify the telemetry that records library loads and file writes.
Explain why a hijacked program may continue to behave normally.
